ENEL 585 – Magnetics

Topic 13

Dr. Philippe Gray

Department of Electrical & Software Engineering

Magnetics: The Plan

The inductor or transformer is often among a converter’s largest and highest-loss components. For a filter inductor, the switching frequency, ripple and load set its inductance and its peak and rms currents, and these set the core and winding it needs.

  1. Magnetic circuits: from the winding’s \(v\), \(i\) through the core’s \(B\), \(H\) to \(L=N^2/\mathcal R\) (\(\mathcal R\): reluctance)
  2. The air gap: it stores the energy, trading inductance for current
  3. Saturation: the maximum flux density, which limits the peak current
  4. Sizing an inductor: core, turns, gap and dc copper area; what \(f\) and ripple change
  5. Lecture 2: copper and core loss, temperature rise, and the transformer

Real Inductors and Transformers

An inductor is a winding of \(N\) turns on a core (material and shape, sometimes a gap); a transformer adds a second winding.

RM10 ferrite core set. A core half (MnZn ferrite), the bobbin the turns go on, a clamp. The worked example’s core size.

Ferrite E core (E42), one half. The bobbin goes on the centre leg; two halves mate at their leg faces.

Powder toroid. Fe-Si-Al alloy powder in a binder (Kool Mµ): a distributed gap, spread by the binder through the material.

Wound toroid inductor. One layer of enamelled copper wire through the ring; \(L=100\ \mu\)H.

Surface-mount power inductor. Core and winding in one part, chosen from its datasheet ratings: inductance, saturation current, dc resistance.

Planar transformer. The windings are copper layers of the circuit board that passes through a flat ferrite core.

Line-frequency (50/60 Hz) transformer. Laminated steel core; primary and secondary side by side on a split bobbin.

Lecture 1 checks an inductor design on an RM10-sized core (first photo). The Core Materials slide compares the materials.

Product photos: DigiKey (TDK, Magnetics, Bourns, Würth Elektronik, Triad Magnetics).

Example: Designing an Inductor

Kassakian Example 18.6: a buck converter’s output filter

Given

\(L=25\ \mu\text{H}\), carrying \(i_L\) between \(9\) and \(11\) A at \(f=500\) kHz (\(T=2\ \mu\)s), so \(I_{\max}=11\) A.

Choose

A core (material and size, with a gap \(g\) if the material needs one; a powder core’s gap is distributed), the number of turns \(N\), and the conductor (wire or PCB copper) and its cross-section.

Within three limits

  1. Flux: at \(I_{\max}\), the core’s flux must stay below the most its material can carry, or \(L\) falls.
  2. Space: the turns must fit in the core’s window, the opening they pass through.
  3. Heat: winding and core losses must not overheat them (Lecture 2).

Next five slides: \(L\) and the core’s flux from \(N\), core size and material.

Magnetic Quantities and Their Electric Analogs

A field along a length, a density through an area

Electric, in a conductor: the field \(E\) along a length \(\ell\) gives the voltage \(V=E\ell\); the current density \(J\) through the cross-section \(A\) gives the current \(I=JA\).

Magnetic field \(H\) (A/m): along a length \(\ell\) it gives the magnetomotive force (MMF) \[ \mathcal F=H\ell\quad\text{(A)} \]

Flux density \(B\) (T): through the cross-section \(A_c\) it gives the flux \[ \Phi=BA_c\quad\text{(Wb = V·s)} \]

Each product assumes a uniform field, along the length or normal to the cross-section.

Next: Faraday’s law links \(\Phi\) to a winding’s voltage, Ampère’s law links \(\mathcal F\) to its current, and the core’s material links \(B\) to \(H\).

Faraday’s Law: From Flux to Voltage

Assumes: all the flux stays in the core, so every turn links the same \(\Phi\). Signs: \(v\), \(i\) and \(\Phi\) as marked.

From the core flux to the winding voltage

  1. One turn around the core, with the flux \(\Phi\) through it: \(\;v_{\text{turn}}=\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}\)
  1. \(N\) turns in series, all linking the same \(\Phi\): \[ v=N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\qquad\Big(\text{Topic 4: }v=\frac{d\lambda}{dt},\ \ \lambda=N\Phi\Big) \]
  1. With \(\Phi=BA_c\): \[ v=NA_c\frac{dB}{dt} \]

Read the other way, the voltage applied to the winding sets how \(B\) changes: \(\;B(t)=B(0)+\dfrac{1}{NA_c}\displaystyle\int_0^t v(\tau)\,d\tau\)

Ampère’s Law: From Current to Field

Assumes: all the flux stays in the core; the same \(A_c\) and material all the way round, slender enough that the field is nearly uniform over \(A_c\).

From the winding current to the field in the core

  1. Ampère: around any closed loop, \(\oint\mathbf H\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=I_{\text{enc}}\), the total current passing through the loop.
  1. The loop: the mean path, of length \(\ell_c\). Each of the \(N\) turns carries \(i\) through it once, so \(I_{\text{enc}}=Ni\).
  1. The field: take \(H\) as its average along the mean path, so \(\oint\mathbf H\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=H\ell_c\) and \[ H\ell_c=Ni \] In FEMM (left) the legs run about 12 % above this average and the corners below it.

The winding is an MMF source: it sets \(\mathcal F=Ni\) around the core, so \(H=Ni/\ell_c\), whatever the material.

Core Material: From Field to Flux Density

Example core: \(\mu_r=2000\), \(B_s=0.3\) T. At \(H=50\) A/m its line gives 0.13 T, air 63 µT: air’s line lies on the \(H\) axis at this scale.

From the field in the core to its flux density

  1. Free space: \(\;B=\mu_0H\), with \(\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\) H/m.
  1. A core material: \(H\) turns its atoms’ magnetic moments toward \(H\). Their magnetization \(M\) (A/m) adds its own flux density: \[ B=\mu_0H+\mu_0M \]
  1. While the core is linear, \(M\propto H\), written \(M=(\mu_r-1)H\): \[ B=\mu_0H+(\mu_r-1)\mu_0H=\mu_r\mu_0H \] \(\mu_r\) is the relative permeability (air: 1; silicon steel and MnZn ferrite: about \(10^3\) to \(10^4\)).
  1. Only below saturation: with nearly all moments aligned, \(B\) nears \(B_s\) and more \(H\) adds little \(B\) (slide 18).

Current first: \(i\to H\) (Ampère) \(\to B\to v\) (Faraday).
Voltage first (transformer): \(v\to B\) (Faraday) \(\to H\to i\) (Ampère).

Around the Map: Inductance

Assumes: all the flux stays in the core; \(B\), and so \(H\), is the same everywhere in the core, so \(\Phi=BA_c\) and \(H=Ni/\ell_c\); \(B\) well below \(B_s\), so \(\mu_r\) is constant; winding resistance neglected.

Around the map, from \(v\) to \(i\) (voltage first)

  1. Faraday, \(\Phi=BA_c\): \(\;v=NA_c\dfrac{dB}{dt}\)
  1. Material: \(\;v=\mu_r\mu_0NA_c\dfrac{dH}{dt}\)
  1. Ampère, \(H=Ni/\ell_c\): \(\;v=\dfrac{\mu_r\mu_0A_cN^2}{\ell_c}\,\dfrac{di}{dt}\)

This is \(v=L\,di/dt\), with \(\;L=\dfrac{\mu_r\mu_0A_cN^2}{\ell_c}\)

\(L\propto N^2\) (\(N\) turns make \(H\), and \(N\) turns link the flux), set by the core’s geometry and material, not by \(i\).

A real core is not uniform (left, one scale): in slide 7’s field solve the legs’ \(H\) runs about 12 % above \(Ni/\ell_c\), and that core’s solved \(L\) is about 13 % above this value. The core is linear, so \(L\) is still a constant; only saturation and hysteresis (later) stop it being one.

Example: A Toroid Inductor

Kassakian Example 18.2: \(N=25\), \(\ell_c=15\) cm, \(A_c=1\ \text{cm}^2\), \(\mu_r=200\).

The last slide’s \(L\), for a ring core

  1. The mean path is the ring’s mean circumference: \(\ell_c=15\) cm.
  1. The inductance: \[ L\approx\frac{\mu_r\mu_0A_cN^2}{\ell_c}=\frac{200\cdot4\pi\times10^{-7}\cdot10^{-4}\cdot25^2}{0.15}=105\ \text{µH} \]
  1. The material: molypermalloy powder (MPP) cores are sold with \(\mu_r=200\) (Magnetics Inc.).
  1. The field is not uniform over \(A_c\): \(H=Ni/(2\pi r)\) is larger near \(r_i\) than near \(r_o\). If the example’s \(A_c\) is square, \(H\) runs from \(1.26\,Ni/\ell_c\) at \(r_i\) to \(0.83\,Ni/\ell_c\) at \(r_o\) (left), yet taking it as uniform gives \(L\) only 1.5 % low (derivation: next slide).

Self-Study: The Exact Inductance of a Toroid

Assumes: a linear core, all the flux in the core, a rectangular cross-section \(h\) by \(r_o-r_i\).

Mean circumference: \(L\) low by 0.4, 1.4, 4, 15 % at \((r_o-r_i)/r_i=0.25\), 0.5, 1, 3.

Adding up thin rings

  1. One thin ring of radius \(r\) and thickness \(dr\): its path is \(2\pi r\) long and its cross-section is \(h\,dr\).
  2. Ampère around it: all \(N\) turns pass through it, so \(H(r)=Ni/(2\pi r)\), largest at \(r_i\).
  3. Its flux is \(d\Phi=\mu_r\mu_0H\,h\,dr\): the rings are flux paths in parallel.
  4. Adding the rings, with \(\ell=2\pi r\), \(H=Ni/\ell\) and \(dA=h\,dr\): \[ L=\frac{N\Phi}{i}=\mu_r\mu_0N^2\!\int\frac{dA}{\ell}=\frac{\mu_r\mu_0hN^2}{2\pi}\ln\frac{r_o}{r_i} \]
  5. Against the mean path: \(\mu_r\mu_0N^2A_c/\ell_c\) uses \(1/\ell_c\), but the integral averages \(1/\ell\), which the short inner rings lift above \(1/\ell_c\): \(L\) comes out low.

Reluctance: The Magnetic Circuit

Electric Magnetic
voltage \(V\) MMF \(\mathcal F\) (a winding: \(Ni\))
current \(I\) flux \(\Phi\)
resistance \(R\) reluctance \(\mathcal R\)
\(V=RI\) \(\mathcal F=\mathcal R\,\Phi\)

MMF drives flux, as voltage drives current

  1. What it gives: the winding’s MMF \(Ni\) drives flux round the core, as a voltage drives current: \(\Phi=\mathcal F/\mathcal R\), where \(\mathcal R\) (A/Wb) is the path’s reluctance.
  1. How to find it: Ampère, \(H\ell_c=Ni\), and the material, \(\Phi=\mu_r\mu_0HA_c\) (slide 8), give \(\Phi=Ni\,\mu_r\mu_0A_c/\ell_c\), so \[ \mathcal R_{\text{core}}=\frac{\ell_c}{\mu_r\mu_0A_c} \] A longer path or smaller \(\mu_rA_c\) gives more, as a longer or thinner wire does (all flux in the core, \(\mu_r\) constant).
  1. Inductance: Faraday, \(v=N\,d\Phi/dt\), with \(\Phi=Ni/\mathcal R_{\text{core}}\), gives \(L=N^2/\mathcal R_{\text{core}}\), as on slide 9.
  1. Why it helps: a gap (next slide) adds its own reluctance in series, and they add like resistors.

Adding a Gap

Why that matters: a core’s \(\mu_r\) changes with temperature, with flux level and from one core to the next.

Example: \(\ell_c=100\) mm, \(g=1\) mm, \(\mu_r=2000\): \(\ell_c/\mu_r=0.05\) mm \(=g/20\), so the gap takes \(1/1.05=95\) % of \(Ni\). If \(\mu_r\) falls to 1000, \(\ell_c/\mu_r\) rises to 0.10 mm and \(L\) falls to \(1.05/1.10=0.955\) of its value, a 4.5 % drop. With no gap, \(L\) would halve.

Gap in series with the core

  1. What the gap does: length \(g\), \(\mu_r=1\), it adds \(\mathcal R_{\text{gap}}=g/(\mu_0A_c)\) in series with \(\mathcal R_{\text{core}}\) (\(\ell_c\) now the path through the core alone), so by slide 12 \[ L=\frac{N^2}{\mathcal R_{\text{core}}+\mathcal R_{\text{gap}}}=\frac{\mu_0A_cN^2}{g+\ell_c/\mu_r} \]
  1. Why the gap dominates: the same \(\Phi\) through the same \(A_c\) gives the same \(B\) in both, but the gap’s \(H=B/\mu_0\) is \(\mu_r\) times the core’s \(B/(\mu_r\mu_0)\). So the gap takes \(g/(g+\ell_c/\mu_r)\) of \(Ni\) (flux spreading past the gap’s edges neglected: ‘What the Simple Model Leaves Out’).
  1. When the gap dominates: if \(g\gg\ell_c/\mu_r\), \(\;L\approx\mu_0A_cN^2/g\), nearly independent of \(\mu_r\).

The Gap Trades Inductance for Current

Same core, same 40 turns; only \(g\) changes

Example core: \(A_c=1\ \text{cm}^2\), slide 13’s \(\ell_c=100\) mm and \(\mu_r=2000\).

Model: \(B=Li/(NA_c)\) up to the saturation flux density \(B_s=0.3\) T, then flat (the real curve bends, slide 8).

  1. A wider gap lowers \(L\), so the same \(i\) makes less \(B\).
  1. Saturation comes at the same \(B_s\), at a larger current: \(B=\Phi/A_c\) with \(\Phi=Ni/(\mathcal R_{\text{core}}+\mathcal R_{\text{gap}})\), so \(B\) reaches \(B_s\) at \(\;I_{\text{sat}}=B_sA_c(\mathcal R_{\text{core}}+\mathcal R_{\text{gap}})/N\).
  1. \(L\) falls and \(I_{\text{sat}}\) rises by the same factor: \(L\propto1/\mathcal R\) and \(I_{\text{sat}}\propto\mathcal R\), so \(LI_{\text{sat}}=NB_sA_c\), the flux linkage at saturation, is the same for every \(g\). From \(g=0\) to 1 mm: \(L\) 4.02 mH → 191 µH and \(I_{\text{sat}}\) 0.30 → 6.27 A (both ×21).

Where the Energy Is Stored

Slide 14’s core at \(I_{\text{sat}}\): \(W=\tfrac12LI_{\text{sat}}^2\) is 0.18 mJ at \(g=0\), 3.76 mJ at \(g=1\) mm. Where is it?

Energy in one piece

\(\Phi=Ni/\mathcal R\) and \(L=N^2/\mathcal R\) give \(\;\tfrac12Li^2=\tfrac12\Phi^2\mathcal R\).

A piece with uniform \(\mu\) and \(B\), length \(\ell\) along \(\Phi\) and area \(A\) (core: \(\ell_c\), \(\mu_r\mu_0\); gap: \(g\), \(\mu_0\)) has \(\mathcal R=\ell/(\mu A)\) and \(\Phi=BA\), so \[ \tfrac12\Phi^2\mathcal R=\frac{B^2}{2\mu}\,A\ell \] an energy density \(w=B^2/2\mu\) times the volume.

Core and gap in series

Same \(\Phi\) in both (and, without fringing, same \(B\)), so \[ W=\tfrac12\Phi^2(\mathcal R_{\text{core}}+\mathcal R_{\text{gap}}) \]

Each piece holds its share of \(\mathcal R\). Slide 13’s gap had 95 %, so it holds 3.58 of the 3.76 mJ.

If \(g\gg\ell_c/\mu_r\): \(\;W\approx\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0}A_cg\)

What a Gap Can Hold

Energy density at \(B_{\max}\)

Core \(B_{\max}\) (design limit) \(B_{\max}^2/2\mu_0\)
iron alloy 1.6 T 1.0 J/cm³
ferrite 0.3 T 0.036 J/cm³

Reading the table

Slide 14’s gap: \(V_g=A_cg=100\ \text{mm}^3=0.1\ \text{cm}^3\); at 0.3 T it holds \(0.036\ \text{J/cm}^3\times0.1\ \text{cm}^3=3.6\) mJ, the 3.58 mJ of slide 15.

The material sets the energy per gap volume: through \(B_{\max}^2\), an iron-alloy gap holds 28× more per cm³ than a ferrite one. Ferrite is still used at high frequency: it is a ceramic, and its high resistivity keeps eddy loss small (Self-Study: Core Materials).

Self-Study: What the Simple Model Leaves Out

2D field solve of the demo core: \(N=40\), \(A_c=1\) cm², \(\ell_c=100\) mm, \(\mu_r=2000\), \(g=1\) mm. Equal flux between neighbouring lines.

Two flux paths the magnetic circuit ignores

  1. Fringing: flux bulges out at the gap, so for the same \(B\) it crosses an area larger than \(A_c\). More flux per amp: \(\mathcal R_{\text{gap}}\) falls and \(L\) rises.
  2. Leakage: some flux closes through the air without crossing the gap. It also raises \(L\).

Fringing is small while \(g\) is under about a tenth of the core’s side (Kassakian). Here \(g=1\) mm in 6 mm legs: the solve gives \(L=326\) µH, the circuit 191 µH. In practice the gap is trimmed to the measured \(L\).

Reading B and H off the Terminals

Demo core, no gap, lossless (\(H_c=0\)), 1 kHz; drag \(t\) or \(V\).

A lossless core first: drive \(v\), record \(i\) and \(v_2\)

  1. \(H\) from \(i\), \(B\) from a sense winding: \(H=N_1i/\ell_c\), \(B=\frac{1}{N_2A_c}\int v_2\,dt\); open, it has no \(iR\) drop. Here \(N_2=N_1\): \(v_2=v\).
  1. 0→1: \(v=+V\) ramps \(B\) up to 0; \(|B|\) falls, so the core gives energy back: \(p=vi<0\).
  1. 1→2: to the tip: energy re-enters, \(p>0\) (blue).
  1. 2→3: \(v\) flips; \(B\) comes back down the same curve: one \(H\) for each \(B\).
  1. 3→4: back to \(-B_{pk}\): the areas cancel, \(\bar P=0\), nothing lost; \(i\) nearly a triangle, as in a buck.
  1. Drive harder: 2.3× the volts: \(i\) spikes as the core saturates, yet \(\bar P\) is still 0. Saturation is not loss.

A Real Core Loses Energy Each Cycle

Same core and drive, now with hysteresis (\(H_c=15\) A/m); drag \(t\) or \(V\).

Same tracer, a real core: \(L\parallel R_c\)

  1. Two branches: the extra \(H\) that moves the domains points the way \(B\) moves, so its current has the sign of \(v\): in the circuit, it flows in \(R_c\).
  1. 0→2: up the right branch: at each \(B\), \(i\) is higher than the lossless core’s.
  1. 2→4: down the left branch, \(i\) lower. Extra current × \(v\) > 0 both ways, so blue outweighs grey: \(\bar P\) = 11 mW, \(f\) × the loop’s area × \(A_c\ell_c\), as heat.
  1. Drive harder: \(\bar P\) = 140 mW (13×). \(R_c=V^2/\bar P\): 520 Ω at 2.4 V, 224 Ω here; it fits one \(V\) and \(f\).
  1. b and c (next slide): at b, \(i=0\) with 0.11 T left; at c, \(B=0\) needs \(H=-15\) A/m.

Self-Study: Core Materials

Representative values (Kassakian Table 18.1 and Section 18.5; Erickson Section 13.3.1)
Material \(B_s\) (T) \(\mu_r\) Resistivity (µΩ·cm) Typical use
Silicon steel (2.5 % Si) 2.0 \(5\times10^3\) 40 line frequency: transformers, motors
50 % cobalt alloy 2.3 \(10^4\) 35 highest \(B_s\), expensive
Metallic glass 1.6 \(10^4\) 125 thin ribbon, brittle
Ferrite (MnZn) 0.4–0.8 \((1\text{–}4)\times10^3\) high (ceramic) power grades, to about 1 MHz
Ferrite (NiZn) 0.3 \(4\)–\(500\) high (ceramic) some grades beyond 30 MHz

The trade: metals saturate at 1.6–2.3 T but conduct, so changing flux drives eddy currents (Lecture 2); ferrites saturate lower but keep eddy loss small at high frequency.

Grade matters: choose by the maker’s loss data at your \(f\), peak \(B\) and temperature.

Filling the Window: the Fill Factor

Sketch of one window’s cross-section, not to scale

What the winding needs

  1. The window \(W_A\): the bobbin’s space for the winding, which every turn passes through (the RM10 photo on slide 3). The winding also fills the window on the other side of the centre leg; \(W_A\) is one window, crossed once by each turn.
  1. A turn takes more than its copper: its insulation and the gaps between round wires. Even bare round wires stacked in a square grid fill only \(\pi/4=79\,\%\) of their squares.
  1. Fill factor \(k_u=\dfrac{NA_w}{W_A}\) (\(A_w\): copper area of one turn), the fraction of the window that is copper. Kassakian’s examples take \(k_u=0.5\) to \(0.64\).
  1. The check: with \(A_{\text{turn}}\) the window area one turn takes, the winding fits if \(NA_{\text{turn}}\le W_A\).

Winding Resistance

Top view, the core’s top half lifted off; sketch, not to scale

From the wire to \(R\)

  1. One turn goes once round the centre leg: part of it lies in the windows, the rest outside the core. Its mean length is \(\ell_t\): 52 mm on an RM10 bobbin.
  1. The wire is \(N\ell_t\) long with copper area \(A_w\), so \[ R=\rho\,\frac{N\ell_t}{A_w} \]
  1. Copper’s resistivity is \(\rho=1.7\times10^{-8}\) Ω·m at 20 °C and rises by 0.39 % of that per °C (Kassakian Eq. 18.36). Windings run hot: at 75 °C, \(\rho\approx2.1\times10^{-8}\) Ω·m (Example 20.1 takes \(2.09\times10^{-8}\)).
  1. The next slide’s winding: \(N\ell_t=11\times52\ \text{mm}=0.572\) m of AWG 15 (\(A_w=1.65\ \text{mm}^2\)), at 12.7 mΩ per metre at 75 °C, so \(R=7.2\) mΩ.

Is This Inductor Design Viable?

Specification (Example 18.6): \(L=25\ \mu\)H, \(I_{\max}=11\) A, \(I_{rms}=10.0\) A, \(B_{\max}=0.3\) T, \(R_{\max}=10\ \text{m}\Omega\)

  1. Inductance: \(L=\frac{\mu_0N^2A_c}{g+\ell_c/\mu_r}=25.3\ \mu\)H ✓
  1. Saturation: flux linkage \(\lambda=NBA_c=Li\) (Topic 4), so \(B_{pk}=\frac{LI_{\max}}{NA_c}=0.29\) T \(\le B_{\max}\) ✓
  1. Window: \(NA_{\text{turn}}=38.5\ \text{mm}^2\le W_A\) ✓, \(k_u=0.44\)
  1. Resistance: \(R=7.2\) mΩ (last slide) \(\le R_{\max}\) ✓; \(I_{rms}^2R=0.73\) W

Viable. Lecture 2 adds ac and core loss, and heat.

The Same Inductor at 250 kHz

What changes from the last slide

Last slide Now
Switching frequency \(f\) 500 kHz 250 kHz
Ripple \(\Delta I\) 2 A (9 to 11 A) 2 A, kept
\(L\) 25 µH 50 µH
\(I_{\max}\) 11 A 11 A
Core and wire unchanged

Why \(L\) doubles: the ripple is \(\Delta I=v_Lt_{\text{on}}/L\), and halving \(f\) doubles the on-time \(t_{\text{on}}\).

In general, \(L\propto1/(f\,\Delta I)\): a higher \(f\) or more ripple lowers \(LI_{\max}\) and allows a smaller core, at the price of more loss (Lecture 2).

  1. Saturation: \(N\ge\frac{LI_{\max}}{A_cB_{\max}}=21.1\), so \(N=22\)
  1. Window: \(NA_{\text{turn}}=77\ \text{mm}^2>W_A=41.5\ \text{mm}^2\) ✗
  1. Thinner wire to fit: \(A_{\text{turn}}=W_A/N=1.89\ \text{mm}^2\); with copper still 47 % of each turn’s area, \(A_w=0.89\ \text{mm}^2\) and \(R=26.9\) mΩ \(>R_{\max}\) ✗

Not viable on this core: a bigger core is needed, with more \(A_c\) (fewer turns) or more window.

One Current, Three Limits

Example 18.6: \(i_L\) from 9 to 11 A at 500 kHz

\(i_L\) is the dc \(I_o=10\) A plus the ripple \(i_L-I_o\), a triangle of \(\Delta I=2\) A peak to peak. Each limit depends on a different part of it.

  1. The peak sets saturation: \(I_{\max}=I_o+\Delta I/2=11\) A, and the design keeps \(LI_{\max}\le NA_cB_{\max}\).
  1. The rms sets winding heat, \(I_{rms}^2R\). The ripple’s rms is \(\Delta I/(2\sqrt3)=0.58\) A (a ramp from \(-\Delta I/2\) to \(+\Delta I/2\)), and it averages to zero, so \(I_{rms}=\sqrt{I_o^2+0.58^2}=10.0\) A.
  1. The ripple sets the flux swing: \(NA_cB=Li_L\), so \(B\) changes only with the ripple, by \(\Delta B=L\,\Delta I/(NA_c)\). Core loss depends on that swing, and the ripple is the only ac part of \(i_L\).

Winding Loss: Hot Copper and Skin Depth

A solid wire the size of the book’s litz bundle, sine current at 500 kHz; \(H_e\) equal to the wire’s own surface field

Dc resistance (Eq. 18.36): \(R=\rho N\ell_t/A_w\), with \(\rho\) at the winding’s working temperature: \(2.09\times10^{-8}\) Ω·m at 75 °C, over 20 % above its value at 20 °C.

Skin effect: an ac current crowds toward a conductor’s surface, into a depth \(\delta=\sqrt{2\rho/(\omega\mu_0)}\) (Eq. 18.37), 0.10 mm in copper at 500 kHz. In a conductor much thicker than \(\delta\) the ac current sees \(F_RR\), with \(F_R=R_{ac}/R>1\) rising with frequency.

Proximity effect: the field of nearby turns, and the gap’s fringing field, also induce eddy currents in a conductor, pushing its current to the side where that field adds to its own; most in windings of several layers and near the gap, raising \(F_R\) further. Litz wire limits both: strands thinner than \(\delta\), each taking every position in the bundle.

Core Loss: Hysteresis, Eddy Currents, Steinmetz

Hysteresis: each trip round the \(B\)-\(H\) loop costs its area, \(\oint H\,dB\), per unit volume, \(f\) times a second (Eq. 18.38). An inductor’s \(B\) swings \(\pm B_{ac}\) about \(B_{dc}\): the minor loop’s area, set mainly by \(B_{ac}\), is the loss; \(B_{dc}+B_{ac}\) stays below \(B_{\max}\).

Eddy currents: a changing \(B\) induces voltages around loops in the core material; the currents they drive heat its resistance. Insulated laminations (steel) cut each loop’s area, and a high-resistivity material (ferrite) its current.

Steinmetz fit (Eq. 18.39): \(P_v=kf^\alpha B_{ac}^\beta\) per unit volume, fitted to one material’s loss: \(k\), \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) belong to the grade, from the maker’s tests with a sine \(B\) over a stated \(f\) and temperature range. The core enters only through its effective volume: \(P_c=P_vV_{c,e}\). With no \(B_{dc}\) term, it only estimates a biased, triangular \(B\).

Loss climbs steeply with the swing: \(\beta\) is typically 1.6 to 3.5. For the plotted ferrite \(\beta=3.54\), so twice \(B_{ac}\) at the same \(f\) is \(2^{3.54}=11.6\) times \(P_v\).

Both losses heat the part (Eq. 20.18): \(\Delta T=R_{th}(P_w+P_c)\) above ambient, \(P_w\) the winding loss, \(R_{th}\) the maker’s typical value for the wound core (it varies with mounting and airflow).

The Transformer: Volt-Seconds Set the Flux

Dots: \(i_1\) in and \(i_2\) out, as in Topic 4

The voltage sets the flux; the current follows

  1. Faraday sets \(B\): \(v_1=N_1A_c\,dB/dt\), so the primary’s volt-seconds alone set the swing of \(B\), whatever the load draws.
  1. Ampère gives the current that \(B\) needs: \(H\ell_c=N_1i_1-N_2i_2\). The reflected part of \(i_1\) (Topic 4) cancels the load’s \(N_2i_2\), leaving \(N_1i_m\): load current adds no flux.
  1. So, usually, no gap: \(i_m=\lambda_1/L_m\), \(L_m=N_1^2/\mathcal R\). A gap raises \(\mathcal R\), so the same volt-seconds draw more \(i_m\), which delivers no power but adds winding loss (Kassakian 18.4.5).
  1. The inductor is the opposite: its whole current magnetizes the core to store energy, so it is gapped. So is the flyback, a coupled inductor storing energy in \(L_m\) (Topic 5).

Designing a Transformer: What Changes

Example 20.2’s transformer: 400 V square wave, 1 A rms, 200 kHz

\(v_1=\pm V_{in}\) for \(T/2\) each (a full bridge): zero volt-seconds per period, so in steady state \(B\) swings evenly about zero.

  1. Volt-seconds set \(B_{pk}\): by \(v_1=N_1A_c\,dB/dt\), one half-period carries \(B\) from \(-B_{pk}\) to \(+B_{pk}\): \(2B_{pk}N_1A_c=V_{in}T/2\), so \(B_{pk}=\frac{V_{in}}{4fN_1A_c}\).
  1. Core loss, not saturation, limits \(B_{pk}\): the flux swings fully every cycle, not as a filter inductor’s small ripple on a dc part, so \(B_{pk}\) is set by the core loss accepted, below \(B_s\). Example 20.2: 0.1 T, where N87 ferrite loses 200 mW/cm³ (200 kHz, 100 °C).
  1. Turns trade core loss for winding loss: on a given core, window full, more turns lower \(B_{pk}\) and core loss but thin the wire, raising winding loss. Example 20.3 (RM14 core): the least, 1.39 W (0.60 core, 0.79 winding), is at \(N_1=48\), \(B_{pk}=59\) mT; a 26 °C rise.
